title: Choose the smallest architecture that protects the constraint
description: Switch constraints to change the active request path, then select a component to inspect what it owns. Each scenario adds only the mechanism needed for that pressure.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: The client starts a request and experiences the result, whether it is fast, stale, limited, or unavailable.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Routes requests to healthy interchangeable application workers so one worker does not define the system's capacity or availability.

nodes.label: Application service
nodes.detail: Validates input, applies the product rule, and decides whether a request can use a cached answer, a fallback, or the authoritative store.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.detail: Serves data that is safe to reuse and reduces repeated read work. It is not the authority for a fact unless the product explicitly says so.

nodes.label: Primary store
nodes.detail: Owns the durable record and the invariant for critical writes. It needs backups even when it has replicas or failover.

nodes.label: Read replica
nodes.detail: Offers another read path when the product can tolerate replication delay. It cannot promise read-after-write freshness by itself.

scenarios.label: Small product
scenarios.summary: A new product has modest traffic and changes weekly. Fast, correct delivery matters more than distributing a workload that has not appeared yet.
scenarios.result: Start with one modular application and one authoritative store. Keep clear code and data boundaries so a measured bottleneck can be isolated later; do not add distributed coordination before it protects a real constraint.

scenarios.label: Traffic growth
scenarios.summary: One application worker is near its latency limit during peak traffic, while requests can be handled independently once the worker state is externalized.
scenarios.result: Add stateless workers behind a load balancer. This removes the single worker as the immediate limit, but the primary store is now the next resource to measure rather than an issue already solved.

scenarios.label: Read-heavy workload
scenarios.summary: Many requests ask for the same data, and the product allows a bounded freshness window for those answers.
scenarios.result: Use a cache for data that is safe to reuse, then size the authoritative store for misses and cache regressions. A high average hit rate is useful only while the miss path remains healthy.

scenarios.label: Critical write
scenarios.summary: A user reserves a limited item. The system must prevent two successful reservations for the last unit even if a client retries after a timeout.
scenarios.result: Keep one authoritative write path with a transaction or conditional update, and use an idempotency key to reconcile retries. Replicas can help lag-tolerant reads, but they do not replace the primary's invariant.
